purpose: Bounded Federal Reserve SHED record connecting income timing, outside help, price pressure, and household adaptation while keeping exact triggers, protected outcomes, and later room open.

events.geography: United States; Federal Reserve Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking 2025
events.date_precision: 2025 survey/reference year; no dated bill, price, employer, or policy episode is identified
events.denominator: U.S. adults; question-specific samples and subgroup denominators vary across income, help, variability, and adaptation measures
events.method: Structured extraction from the Federal Reserve's official 2025 SHED published household-finance tables and report
events.missingness: Respondent identity across a dated episode, bill or price, receipt timing, liquid balance, debt terms, family-help amount, care obligations, schedule control, provider response, remedy, trust, switching, and exit are not retained
events.exposure: 30% of adults reported income varying at least occasionally; 11% reported that variability made it difficult to pay bills; 23% reported outside help with a listed expense; 41% said money was left over always or often, falling to 19% below $25,000 family income and rising to 59% at $100,000 or more
events.alternatives_before_action: Households reported or could use cheaper products, reduced use, delayed purchases, reduced saving, borrowing, working more, outside help, public assistance, or family support; the survey does not identify the feasible set for one episode
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: Price-response reports included switching to cheaper products (62%), using less or stopping use (60%), delaying a major purchase (46%), reducing saving (41%), borrowing more (16%), and working more or getting another job (17%); categories can overlap
events.choice_or_response: Respondents reported combinations of switching, reducing use, delaying, saving less, borrowing, working more, and receiving help; these may represent smoothing, deprivation, preference, or mixed motives
events.person_or_actor_with_control: Households make adaptations, while employers, pay schedules, prices, lenders, providers, family networks, and public programs shape the available room; the survey does not identify control in a specific case
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: The published survey reports income, help, and adaptation conditions but does not link a provider, employer, lender, agency, or firm remedy to a particular respondent episode
events.immediate_outcome: Financial pressure is converted into different combinations of visible spending, reduced consumption, delayed purchases, lower saving, borrowing, extra work, and outside help
events.protected_outcome: Adaptations may protect current food, housing, health, or consumption, and outside help may prevent an immediate missed expense; the protected outcome is not identified for each respondent
events.sacrificed_outcome: Households may sacrifice quality, savings, time, care, rest, health, future flexibility, or independence; the survey does not assign each sacrifice to a named person or adaptation
events.cost_risk_transfer: A bill or price constraint can transfer risk into depleted savings, debt, additional labor, unpaid family support, lower-quality consumption, or delayed care; the source does not identify the full balance
events.later_outcome: The survey does not follow a dated household episode to later cash room, repayment, health, housing, care, work, trust, switching, or exit
events.meaning_and_attribution: The source measures financial condition and reported adaptation, not fairness, blame, dignity, institutional trust, or cultural meaning for the same episode
events.public_or_collective_response: No respondent-linked complaint, organizing, policy demand, political action, or collective response is joined to the adaptation reports
events.counterexample: Working more can protect current consumption while reducing care or rest; low paid spending can reflect inability to buy an alternative rather than low need; outside help can buffer a bill without creating durable room
events.source_and_uncertainty: Official Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published estimates, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-income-expenses.htm; descriptive self-reports, not a dated event study or causal estimate

arrows.from: income timing, price pressure, or limited budget margin
arrows.to: difficulty paying bills or need for outside help
arrows.evidence: The SHED tables report income variability, bill difficulty attributed to variability, outside help, and income-patterned budget margin
arrows.counterexample: Income variability can be absorbed by savings, benefits, credit, or flexible timing; outside help can be ordinary sharing rather than crisis relief
arrows.remaining_gap: Dated bill, amount, receipt timing, liquid buffer, and household-specific mechanism

arrows.to: switching, reduced use, delay, lower saving, borrowing, or working more
arrows.evidence: The official 2025 SHED report publishes each of these price-response categories
arrows.counterexample: Categories overlap and do not reveal whether an adaptation was strategic smoothing, deprivation, or preference
arrows.remaining_gap: Specific trigger, feasible alternative, effort/time cost, and adaptation order

arrows.to: protected consumption or immediate bill payment
arrows.evidence: The survey measures adaptation and help receipt but does not link either to a named protected expense or successful payment
arrows.counterexample: Borrowing or working more can preserve current consumption while moving cost into debt, care, health, or future time
arrows.remaining_gap: Payment completion, amount, quality, time, debt, care, and protected/sacrificed outcome

arrows.to: restored financial room, later security, trust, switching, or exit
arrows.evidence: The published cross-sectional SHED layer does not follow a dated episode to later room, repayment, trust, or exit
arrows.counterexample: A household can report a current surplus while lacking the room to absorb a health, care, housing, or provider shock
arrows.remaining_gap: Same-unit dated follow-up with amount, adequacy, repayment, later security, attribution, trust, switching, and exit

boundary: This ledger formalizes household financial room as a set of distinct buffers and adaptations. It does not establish a dated causal shock, a household recovery rate, or whether any adaptation protected long-term security.
storage_boundary: No SHED microdata or respondent identifiers are retained; only compact official published estimates and explicit open downstream arrows are represented.
